4,843 backtested trading strategies.

Free.

Ranked by Sharpe ratio. The top one sits at 3.39.

→ every strategy tested over decades of real data
→ Sharpe ratio, t stat and years tested for each one
→ full Python code and data
→ 136 libraries for backtesting, bots, market data and broker APIs
→ 55 trading books, beginner to pro

1. Pick from the 61 strongest strategies, sorted by market: stocks, bonds, forex or crypto

2. Create a free account to unlock the Python code and data

3. Paste the code into Claude Code and ask Opus to explain every rule in plain English. When it buys. When it sells. Why.

4. Ask Opus to rerun the backtest with REAL fees on the last 3 years. If it doesn't make money after costs, stop here.

5. Have Opus convert the research code into live code that reads real prices and fires real signals

6. Connect a broker from the libraries, like Alpaca for stocks or Binance for crypto

7. Add a risk layer: fixed position size, a stop loss on every trade, a daily loss limit and a kill switch

8. Paper trade for 2 weeks with fake money. If live results don't match the backtest, the strategy isn't ready.

9. Add Telegram alerts so your phone pings on every trade. Only then go live, and start small.

A great backtest is a starting point, not a promise.

Most strategies die in step 4 or step 8.

That's the point. Better they die there than with your money.

Google's engineers stopped letting AI grade its own homework, and they open-sourced how

it's called the Elephant-Goldfish Model, and Google says thousands of its engineers run it every day on production code

the elephant is one long-running session that remembers everything: the architecture, the intent, every small decision. 

it never writes code. it interviews you, argues with you and keeps the record

the goldfish are fresh sessions with zero memory. they never saw the design talk, so they don't inherit its blind spots

the workflow:
1. brainstorm - you and the elephant debate options under a strict no-code rule
2. draft - a markdown design doc with the problem, the plan, the alternatives and the exact files to change
3. explain back - one goldfish has to explain the design. if it gets it wrong, the doc is ambiguous and goes back
4. attack - several goldfish hunt edge cases, hidden dependencies and logic gaps
5. go/no-go - a last goldfish checks that every file path, data structure and function signature is spelled out

AI made coding faster and made slop faster too. this moves the attack to before the first line of code exists

the trade-offs: it only runs inside Antigravity for now, and the default reviewer list skips security, so you add your own security goldfish

free, Apache 2.0. the model writes the code, the harness decides what ships, and how one engineer actually works with agents day to day is below:

Harness engineering is the most f**king dangerous thing I have seen this year, and anyone can do it.

Four engineers opened the source code of 11 real coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenHands, Aider, Minara and more) and read 4 million lines to answer one question: what is an agent, actually.

Their answer fits in three words: Agent = Model + Harness.

The model is rented. The harness is everything around it, and that is where the money is.

Every one of the 11 systems is built from the same 7 parts:

-> The loop: think, act, check, repeat until done or stopped.
-> The bridge to the model: sends the prompt, reads the tool calls back.
-> Tools: files, code, terminal, whatever the agent can actually touch.
-> Memory and context: what it keeps, what it loads, what it squeezes when the window fills.
-> Safety: what runs on its own, what asks you first, what never runs.
-> Orchestration: sub-agents that split big jobs. The smallest harness skips this entirely.
-> Extensibility: hooks, skills, plugins and MCP, new power without touching the core.

Minara Harness is the same 7 parts pointed at markets: idea -> research -> strategy code -> backtest -> execution in one window.

What shocked them:

> Not one of the 11 runtimes imports LangChain, LangGraph or AutoGen. Four million lines, zero frameworks.
> Not one uses vector search to find code. It is ripgrep, globs and markdown files.
> Skills (SKILL.md) are in more systems than MCP now, 9 of 11 against 8 of 11.

The part for builders: 18 design recommendations and a 90-line starter harness that covers 10 of them.

90 lines. That is the whole entry ticket, for a coding agent or a trading one.

> make 3 cover options for this week's best post, plus a 6 second loop of the winner.

> package the bots that work as shareable templates. strip anything personal.

what i'd do better this time:

→ one chief of staff, not 98 loose bots

→ the gate on day one, not after a scare

→ a weekly audit, not when the bill spikes

→ fewer, sharper routines

→ dashboards over notifications

which room would you build first? 👇

Anthropic built a system where a single sentence takes longer to render than a full specification.

A request like a wooden chair with thin legs carries nine decisions nobody involved ever wrote down.

> ASK - wording two modellers would read apart
> FILL - gaps closed as assumptions, not choices
> BUILD - geometry from the spec, not the sentence
> MARK - assumptions left visible on the object
> HOLD - nothing modelled while meaning splits
> LOG - every refusal written to the same file

Rejection is the mechanism. Nothing gets modelled while the description still allows two separate readings.

Thin is one of those words. The system picks a figure, writes it onto the object, and waits to be corrected.

That figure is what replaced the team, not the geometry. Geometry was never the slow half of this job.

What vanished is the translation layer, the hours spent turning a vague request into something buildable.

A modeller who disagrees argues with a written assumption instead of a finished object nobody can unwind.

ChatGPT users are now reportedly being routed to GPT-6.2 Sol, and the 3D demos are wild. Here's what you need to know.

Token Gremlin (@TokenGremlin) posted at 6:45 PM on Nov 8, 2026 that he is being routed to GPT-6.2 Sol. The post has over 84K views. He says it is outperforming Claude Opus 5.5 in his one-shot design and 3D tests so far.

His demo is a black hole, which he calls the best AI-generated one he has seen. It was generated in one shot, built with Three.js, and packed inside a single HTML file. These are scenes from a single prompt, not game screenshots.

This follows the delay we covered yesterday. GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra missed the Nov 7 date The Information had floated. Now some users say routing has started quietly, so a release next week looks likely to them.

How people say they check it: ask GPT-6.1 Sol, with no web search, whether it knows Fable 5. If it answers, you are reportedly routed to 6.2 Sol. One user says it is fast and uses few tool calls, but at xhigh in Codex he found Astra still better.

Doubts remain. One account says this is just GPT-6.1 Sol. Another stresses it is a rumour and that OpenAI has confirmed nothing.

Key numbers:
- 84.6K views on the main post
- One prompt, one shot, one HTML file
- Built with Three.js
- Predicted by one user: Sol on Mon Nov 9, Astra on Thu Nov 12, with prices about 50% below Claude
- Reported pricing target for Sol: under $2 per million tokens, per infrastructure reports
- Claude Opus 5.5 scores 86.32 vs 78.09 for GPT-6 Sol on one public comparison

OpenAI has not announced GPT-6.2 Sol or Astra, and there is no official release date.

THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls
→ you stop spending Opus on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5
> docs pulls the API reference on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the whole transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

outsiders.text:
THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just listed a pairing in Claude Code that costs less than running Sonnet and still puts Opus on every big call.

The idea: Haiku 5.5, the fastest and cheapest model, drives the whole session, and Opus 5.5 waits on call as the advisor for the decisions that decide the outcome.

The docs put it plainly: more than Haiku alone, less than switching your main model to Sonnet or Opus.

You just start Claude Code like this:

claude --model haiku --advisor opus

this is how it splits:

→ Haiku 5.5 drives the session, edits the files and runs the tests
→ Haiku 5.5 subagents search the repo and report only the failures
→ Opus 5.5 waits on call and reads the full transcript only when Claude asks
→ you pay Haiku rates for the typing and Opus rates only for the thinking

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan gets locked
→ when the same error comes back twice
→ before Claude calls the task done

Haiku types. Haiku digs. Opus thinks.

JEV engineering is the same idea one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) get settled by JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that actually split

the full tree
> Haiku 5.5 runs the main session and applies every fix
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds every call site on Haiku 5.5
> test-runner runs the suite on Haiku 5.5 and reports only failures
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the full transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Haiku 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three read-only Haiku 5.5 subagents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), test-runner (runs the suite, reports only failures).
3. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: consult the advisor before a plan locks, after the same error twice, and before a task is marked done.
4. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. Nothing gets edited until I say go."

needs Claude Code v2.1.293 or later, run claude update first.

↳ https://t.co/vOifNVkwn9

save it, this is the cheapest Opus brain you can plug in.
